 As SNAP Shrinks, Nearly 1.3 Million New Yorkers Rely on Food Pantries and More Than Half Are Working Or Live With Someone Who Does
 Poverty Tracker report shows pantries lift about 51,000 New Yorkers out of poverty
 NEW YORK, NY (November 16, 2026) – Nearly 1.3 million New Yorkers, about 15% of the city, turned to a food pantry or other free food provider in 2025, according to Spotlight on Food Assistance and the Poverty Shortfall in New York City , a new Poverty Tracker report from Robin Hood and Columbia University’s Center on Poverty and Social Policy . The report, released today during a press conference at Food Bank For New York City, finds that pantry users are a broad cross-section of the city, and that more than half of them (55%) are working or live with a spouse or partner who works. 
 The report’s data run through 2025 and do not yet fully capture federal cuts to programs like SNAP, but the authors note that many families will lose access to benefits as those cuts play out, and some will turn to the pantry system to help fill the gap. 
 Key findings 
 Not having enough to eat is commonplace for nearly one-third of New Yorkers.  31% of New Yorkers, more than 2.6 million people, experienced food hardship in 2025, meaning they sometimes or often ran out of food or worried it would run out before they had money to buy more. About 500,000 New Yorkers, 6% of the city, experienced severe food hardship. 
 Pantries are essential infrastructure for New Yorkers in need, including those who work . 55% of pantry users are working or live with a spouse or partner who works. Among the 45% who are not, most are past working age (18%) or have a severe health problem (19%). Only 6% are working-age adults who did not work and reported no health problems. 
 Work should be enough to put food on the table. For too many New Yorkers, it isn’t. Nearly half of pantry users (47%) experienced a major financial shock in a typical year, such as losing a job or public benefits, a sharp drop in income, or an unexpected major expense. One in five experienced a major health shock. 
 Pantry users face multiple hardships. Three-quarters (74%) experienced at least one other material hardship, such as housing instability, energy insecurity, financial problems, or going without medical care because of cost. Contrary to some public perceptions, only 3% have recently experienced a spell of homelessness, though the Poverty Tracker may underrepresent New Yorkers without regular housing. 
 Pantries look like the city, with some differences. Pantry users are more likely to be older adults, families with children, and members of groups with higher poverty rates. 
 Pantries lift families out of poverty, but they have limits. The value of the food distributed by pantries lifts about 51,000 New Yorkers out of poverty. If every pantry user and every New Yorker facing food hardship used pantries weekly, a quarter of a million New Yorkers or more could be lifted out of poverty. That would take a major increase in capacity and would still fill only about 15% of the cost of lifting every New Yorker out of poverty. 
 “Work should be enough to put food on the table. For too many New Yorkers, it isn’t,” said Richard R. Buery, Jr., CEO of Robin Hood. “Pantries are now essential, and they feed 1.3 million New Yorkers and lift about 51,000 out of poverty. But they cannot absorb cuts to SNAP on their own. We must protect the programs that keep New Yorkers fed and make sure the pantries that catch people when other supports fall away have the resources to meet rising needs.” 
 The report emphasizes that the pantry system is best seen as a complement to, not a substitute for, public food assistance such as SNAP and WIC. 
 “Our data show that pantry users look a lot like New York City as a whole, and that more than half are working or live with someone who works. They turn to pantries when budgets are stretched thin, and life knocks them off balance. Pantries make a real difference, but our findings also show their limits. They complement public food assistance and cannot replace it,” said Christopher T. Wimer, Director of the Center on Poverty and Social Policy at Columbia University and a co-author of the report. 
 The context: changes to SNAP 
 The report arrives amid a changing federal landscape for SNAP. According to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, national SNAP participation dropped in June 2026 to its lowest point in 17 years. In New York City, about 26,500 New Yorkers lost SNAP benefits on October 1, even after the city’s outreach helped more than 220,000 New Yorkers keep their benefits. New York State also potentially faces a $1.2 billion state match for SNAP beginning in 2027, about 12 times what the state spends on its food pantry networks.  
 Robin Hood is urging Congress to delay the cost shift for all states during the upcoming lame duck session and, in any final bipartisan Farm Bill, to delay it by two years without a deeper cut to SNAP to offset the cost. In 2025, Robin Hood invested $5.8 million to alleviate food insecurity and promote better nutrition for lower-income New Yorkers through ten emergency food providers. 
 “Every day, we see New Yorkers doing everything right, yet still struggling to put food on the table,” said Leslie Gordon, President and CEO of Food Bank For New York City. “The Robin Hood findings reflect what we see across the communities we serve – one unexpected expense can push a family into crisis. Those who turn to pantries are our neighbors, our coworkers, and families working hard to make ends meet. Food Bank For NYC and its network are a critical lifeline, but we cannot meet this growing need alone. Continued investment in emergency food programs and the broader safety net is essential to ensure New Yorkers have access to the food and support they need.” 
 What the report recommends 
 The report calls for policy actions that reinforce the resources free food providers can count on and help New Yorkers access the programs they are entitled to: 
 Tax credits and accounts: make sure all eligible families get federal and state refundable tax credits and can use tax-advantaged accounts, including the Earned Income Tax Credit, Trump Accounts, and the Empire State Child Credit. 
 SNAP Navigators: fund more Navigators to help families apply for and keep SNAP benefits. 
 Emergency food: boost funding for pantries and other emergency food providers, including through the Hunger Prevention and Nutrition Assistance Program, Nourish NY, and Community Food Connection. 
 WIC: give the program more funding to update and stabilize its operations and reach more eligible New Yorkers. 
 EBT security: ensure a smooth switch to chip and tap-to-pay cards and create a fund to repay families who lost SNAP benefits to theft. 
 SNAP benefit levels: raise minimum SNAP benefits and find other ways to give families the money they need for food, regardless of citizenship status. 
 The report was authored by Daniel Salgado, Christopher Wimer, Yajun Jia, Schuyler Ross, and Christopher Yera of Columbia University. Read the full report here . 
 About the Poverty Tracker 
 Since 2012, the Poverty Tracker has surveyed a representative sample of 3,000 New York households multiple times a year, providing critical longitudinal insight into the dynamics of poverty and disadvantage in the city, tracking employment, assets and debts, health, and more. The Poverty Tracker is a joint project of Robin Hood and Columbia University’s Center on Poverty and Social Policy. 
 About Robin Hood 
 We are NYC’s largest local poverty-fighting philanthropy, and since 1988, we have invested $3 billion to elevate and fuel New Yorkers’ permanent escapes from poverty. In 2025, through $140 million in grantmaking to 295 community partners, we created pathways to opportunity through strategic partnerships on child care, child poverty, jobs, living wages, and more. We are scaling impact at a population level for the more than two million New Yorkers living in poverty. At Robin Hood, we believe your starting point in life should not define where you end up. To learn more about our work and impact, please visit robinhood.org and follow us on Instagram , LinkedIn , Facebook , YouTube , and X . 
 About Columbia University’s Center on Poverty and Social Policy 
 The Center on Poverty and Social Policy at the Columbia University School of Social Work produces actionable research to advance our understanding of poverty and the role of social policy in reducing poverty and promoting economic security, opportunity, and well-being in New York City and the United States. For the center’s latest work and policy briefs, visit   povertycenter.columbia.edu and sign up for research updates . Email at cpsp@columbia.edu . Follow on LinkedIn and Bluesky . 
 About Food Bank For New York City 
 Driven by our mission to empower every New Yorker to achieve food security for good, we harness the collective power of our network of food providers, partners, and volunteers to activate the right resources, supports, and expertise across the five boroughs. Our work with more than 800 soup kitchens, food pantries, and campus partners provides immediate and reliable access to food, while our economic empowerment programs give people the tools and know-how to improve their financial wellness. Community by community, we work together to make progress on a more hopeful, dignified, and equitable future for all. To learn more about our impact or get involved, visit foodbanknyc.org .
